passages.text: A nautical cable is a band of tightly woven and clamped ropes, of a defined cable length, used during the age of sail for deep water anchoring, heavy lifting, ship to ship transfers and towing during blue sea sailing and other uses.

Ordinary rope is not waterproof. When a ship anchors in relatively deep water (greater than about 35 metres or 20 fathoms), the anchor and rope that is let down becomes drenched with water, becoming prohibitively difficult to raise again, even with a mechanism like a capstan. This ultimately limits the depths available with ordinary rope to within the weight bearing capacity of the rope. The rope will become so heavy with water it will break.

The traditional instructions, according to the British Royal Navy in the age of sail, are: Three large strands of tightly woven rope of about 200 metres (110 fathoms) in length are themselves tightly woven in a direction counter to the weave, or twist, of the rope and clamped together over intervals to provide one strong length of rope that is effectively waterproof. The three ropes are so tightly wound counter to the weave of the constituent ropes that the fibers are compressed and the individual weaves stressed, sealing out the water and resulting in a length of about 180 metres (100 fathoms), the UK traditional definition of cable length. Using a cable, the raising of the anchor, or any activity involving submerging the cable, is not more strenuous than lowering.

Hawsers are not cables. Hawsers are ropes of arbitrary length woven together to increase the strength of the overall line, but are not considered waterproof as the weave of the hawser goes with the weave of the constituent ropes. This has come to be known as "hawser laid" and "cable laid". Confusion between cables and hawsers is rampant because both cables and hawsers can be used through the hawsehole.

alignments.label: definition

britannica.quote: CABLE, a thick, large, frong rope, commonly of horn, which fever to keep a flap at anchor.

wikipedia.quote: A nautical cable is a band of tightly woven and clamped ropes, of a defined cable length, used during the age of sail for deep water anchoring, heavy lifting, ship to ship transfers and towing during blue sea sailing and other uses.

alignments.note: Both sources describe a cable as a rope used to hold a vessel at anchor, but Wikipedia defines it as tightly woven and clamped ropes of a defined length used for anchoring and other purposes, while Britannica describes it as a thick, large rope commonly of horn/hemp used to keep a ship at anchor.

alignments.label: quantity

britannica.quote: There is no merchant-thup, however weak, but has at half three cables;

alignments.note: None of the passages mention merchant ships or state how many cables a vessel must carry; they only define cables and hawsers or discuss rope waterproofing and anchoring depths.

alignments.label: practice

britannica.quote: Cable is alfo fluid of ropes, which fever to nife heavy loads, by the help of Granatry pulling, and other engines.

wikipedia.quote: A nautical cable is a band of tightly woven and clamped ropes, of a defined cable length, used during the age of sail for deep water anchoring, heavy lifting, ship to ship transfers and towing during blue sea sailing and other uses.

alignments.note: Both sources describe cables as being made of ropes and used for heavy lifting; the Wikipedia passage confirms the same essential fact without contradicting the historical claim.

alignments.label: quantity

britannica.quote: The name of cable is finally given to dish as have, at leal, three inches in diameter;

alignments.note: The Wikipedia passages describe nautical cables by length (about 180 metres/100 fathoms) and construction from three woven strands, but none mention a three-inch diameter or any naming rule based on diameter.

alignments.label: definition

britannica.quote: thofe that are left as one only called ropes of different names, according to their site.

alignments.note: The Wikipedia passages describe nautical cables, ordinary rope waterproofing limits, and cable construction, but none address ropes receiving different names according to their site or position.

alignments.label: definition

britannica.quote: Every cable, of what thickness forever it be, is com-poded of three friends, every friend of three ropes; and every rope of three twiffs

alignments.note: None of the passages state that a cable is composed of three friends, each of three ropes, and each rope of three twiffs; W3 only mentions three strands being woven together without that specific hierarchical detail.

alignments.label: practice

britannica.quote: they ufe flicks, which they pails frit between the ropes of which they make the lizards

alignments.note: The Wikipedia passages describe nautical cables and hawsers—their construction, waterproofing, length, and uses—but none mentions flicks, plaiting between ropes, or the making of lizards, so the claim is not covered.

alignments.label: practice

britannica.quote: and alfo, to prevent them from twinning or intangling, they hang.

alignments.note: None of the Wikipedia passages mention hanging ropes or cables to prevent twinning or tangling; they address cable construction, waterproofing, length, and the cable/hawser distinction instead.
